faqs.question: Can KDP accept RGB PDFs?
faqs.answer: Yes, many KDP creators upload RGB PDFs, especially from Canva and other design tools. However, printed color will not look identical to a backlit RGB screen. Very bright blues, greens, neon colors, deep blacks, and saturated gradients can shift or print duller. The practical requirement is not simply RGB versus CMYK; it is whether the PDF previews correctly, uses print-safe contrast, and produces acceptable proof-copy results.

faqs.question: What PDF version is best for KDP?
faqs.answer: KDP does not require most beginners to choose a specific PDF version manually. The safer advice is to export a print-ready PDF from your source software using a high-quality print or PDF/X-style preset when available. Avoid experimental PDF features, converter chains, live transparency where unnecessary, and files repeatedly re-saved through multiple tools. The final PDF should open cleanly, preserve dimensions, embed fonts, and preview reliably.

faqs.question: Do fonts need to be embedded for KDP?
faqs.answer: Yes. For best results, fonts should be embedded or embedded as subsets in the PDF. If fonts are not embedded, KDP may substitute them, render text differently, or reject the file during validation. In Acrobat, check File Properties and the Fonts tab. If a font cannot be embedded because of licensing restrictions, use another font or carefully outline display text when appropriate.

faqs.question: How large can a KDP PDF be?
faqs.answer: KDP can handle large PDFs, but large does not automatically mean print-ready. Very large files are more likely to upload slowly, freeze Previewer, or fail processing. Image-heavy coloring books, photo books, and Canva interiors should be optimized by sizing images near 300 DPI at final print size, flattening finished pages, and avoiding unnecessary transparent PNGs. Preserve quality, but remove useless file weight.

faqs.question: Can Canva PDFs be uploaded to KDP?
faqs.answer: Yes. Canva PDFs can work well on KDP if exported correctly. Use the correct custom dimensions, set up bleed when required, keep important content inside safe areas, use PDF Print export, and inspect the final PDF dimensions before upload. Canva does not automatically guarantee correct KDP trim size, cover wrap size, spine width, or safe margin placement.

faqs.question: Why does KDP reject my PDF if it opens correctly?
faqs.answer: Opening correctly only proves the PDF is viewable. KDP checks whether the file can be printed, trimmed, bound, previewed, and reviewed. A PDF can open normally while still having the wrong page size, missing bleed, unsafe text, unembedded fonts, low-resolution images, a cover/interior mismatch, barcode conflict, or corrupted export data. KDP validation is stricter than a desktop PDF viewer.

faqs.question: What is bleed in a KDP PDF?
faqs.answer: Bleed is extra artwork that extends past the final trim edge so edge-to-edge images, backgrounds, or illustrations reach the physical paper edge after cutting. KDP trims printed pages, so artwork that stops exactly at trim can leave a white border. Text, page numbers, logos, and important content should not sit in bleed because bleed can be cut away.

faqs.question: Do coloring books need bleed?
faqs.answer: Coloring books need bleed only when artwork, backgrounds, borders, or patterns are intended to reach the edge of the page. If every illustration sits safely inside white margins, no bleed can be appropriate. Border-heavy coloring books need extra caution because thin edge borders can trigger safe-area problems and make trim variation obvious after printing.

faqs.question: Can I upload PNG instead of PDF to KDP?
faqs.answer: For print interiors, a PDF is the safest and most common upload format. PNG files may be useful as source artwork or for certain cover-building workflows, but a manuscript made from individual PNG pages should usually be assembled and exported as a print-ready PDF. A PDF preserves page order, dimensions, fonts, and production structure better than a folder of images.

faqs.question: How do I check PDF dimensions before uploading to KDP?
faqs.answer: Open the exported PDF in Adobe Acrobat, Preview, or another PDF viewer and check document properties or page size. Compare the PDF dimensions against your selected KDP trim size and bleed setting. For covers, compare the full wrap size against KDP's cover calculator/template for the exact trim size, page count, paper type, and binding.

faqs.question: Does the cover PDF have different requirements than the manuscript PDF?
faqs.answer: Yes. The manuscript PDF is the interior page sequence. The cover PDF is a full wrap that includes back cover, spine, front cover, bleed, safe areas, and barcode space. The cover dimensions depend on trim size, page count, paper type, and binding. Changing the manuscript page count can make the old cover PDF invalid because the spine width changes.

faqs.question: Should I include crop marks in a KDP PDF?
faqs.answer: Usually no. KDP expects the PDF page dimensions themselves to match the required trim or cover size. Extra crop marks can confuse file dimensions or appear as unwanted marks if exported incorrectly. Use KDP templates as locked guide layers in your design software, then remove or hide guide layers and export a clean PDF without printer marks unless a specific KDP workflow requires otherwise.

summary: A KDP PDF must be print-ready, not merely viewable.
The most important requirements are trim size, bleed, safe area, margins, gutter, fonts, image resolution, cover size, spine width, barcode clearance, and clean print export.
The safest workflow is to validate the exported PDF before upload because KDP checks the PDF, not the source design file.

Interior PDF page dimensions match bleed or no-bleed setup.

content: Many creators think: "If my PDF opens correctly, KDP will accept it."
That assumption is understandable. A PDF feels like a finished file. It opens in Preview. It opens in Acrobat. Canva exports it without complaint. The pages look right on screen.

But Amazon KDP is not only checking whether the PDF can open. KDP must upload it, validate its structure, compare dimensions, generate Previewer output, print it, trim it, bind it, and review it. A PDF can look perfect on your computer and still fail one of those production checks.

That is why creators run into upload failures, Previewer errors, print quality issues, margin warnings, bleed problems, cover-size mismatches, and PDF rejections. The file is viewable, but it is not fully print-ready.

This guide explains the practical KDP PDF requirements for manuscripts and covers: trim size, bleed, safe area, margins, gutter, fonts, resolution, color, file size, barcode, spine width, and pre-upload validation.
## Quick PDF Requirements Checklist
Before uploading a PDF to Amazon KDP, confirm these essentials:
- Correct trim size.
- Correct bleed dimensions.
- Safe area respected.
- Fonts embedded.
- High-resolution images.
- Proper page count.
- Correct cover size.
- Correct spine width.
- PDF print export.
- File optimized.
If any item is uncertain, stop and verify it before uploading. Repeated upload attempts do not fix incorrect PDF geometry.
## What Amazon KDP Actually Checks

KDP's PDF checks happen in layers. The upload stage confirms KDP can receive the file. File-structure checks look for a valid PDF, readable pages, usable fonts, and supported content. Dimension checks compare the PDF against the trim size, bleed setting, and cover template. Preview generation renders the book so you can inspect it. Print-readiness checks look for production risks. Review may still catch issues after Previewer opens.
In simple terms:
1. Upload validation.
2. File structure.
3. Dimensions.
4. Bleed.
5. Preview generation.
6. Print readiness.
7. Review.

This is why a successful upload is not the same as approval. A PDF may upload, then fail Previewer. Or it may preview, then fail review. If you are dealing with upload failure specifically, see [KDP File Upload Failed](/blog/kdp-file-upload-failed). If KDP keeps rejecting the PDF after upload, see [Why Amazon KDP Keeps Rejecting My PDF](/blog/why-amazon-kdp-keeps-rejecting-my-pdf).

Official KDP references worth keeping open are [Set Trim Size, Bleed, and Margins](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/GVBQ3CMEQW3W2VL6/), [Format Your Paperback](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G201834190), [Save Your Manuscript File](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G202145060), [Fix Paperback and Hardcover Formatting Issues](https://kdp.amazon.com/en_US/help/topic/G201834260), the [Cover Calculator and Templates](https://kdp.amazon.com/cover-templates?language=en_US), and KDP's [Barcode guidance](https://kdp.amazon.com/help/topic/G5HDYGP4BXLX4RUW).
## Manuscript PDF Requirements
The manuscript PDF is the interior of the book. It includes front matter, body matter, and back matter. For print books, it must match the trim size and bleed setting selected in KDP.

The most important manuscript requirements are page size, page count, margins, and gutter. Page size is the actual PDF page box. Trim size is the finished book size after cutting. If the book has no bleed, the PDF page size usually matches the trim size. If the interior has bleed, the PDF page size must be larger than trim because artwork extends past the cut edge.

Margins protect content from trim variation. The gutter protects content from the binding. As page count increases, gutter becomes more important because the binding curve hides more of the inner page. A 60-page book and a 500-page book should not use the same inner margin.

Example: a 6 x 9 novel with no bleed should have interior pages sized for 6 x 9, with comfortable margins and a sufficient gutter. A 6 x 9 children's book with artwork reaching the edge needs a bleed-sized PDF and artwork extended past trim. A planner with tables and page numbers near the edge must keep those elements inside the safe area.

If your interior triggers a margin warning, use [KDP Margin Too Small Error](/blog/fix-kdp-margin-too-small-error). If the PDF looks fine on screen but prints wrong, read [Why Your KDP PDF Looks Fine on Screen but Prints Wrong](/blog/kdp-pdf-looks-fine-on-screen-but-prints-wrong).
## Cover PDF Requirements
A KDP cover PDF is not only the front cover. For paperbacks and hardcovers, the print cover is usually a full wrap: back cover, spine, front cover, and bleed.

The exact cover size depends on binding type, trim size, interior paper type, page count, and bleed. This is why KDP provides the cover calculator and downloadable templates. If the manuscript page count changes, the spine width changes. If the paper type changes, the spine width may change. If the trim size changes, the whole wrap changes.

A cover PDF must also respect safe areas. Title, subtitle, author name, logos, back-cover text, and spine text should not sit too close to trim or fold edges. The barcode area on the back cover should remain clear of important text or graphics unless you are supplying a compliant barcode workflow.

Common cover errors include front-cover-only PDFs, wrong spine width, old templates, barcode conflicts, unsafe spine text, and backgrounds that do not extend into bleed. For specific fixes, see [KDP Cover Dimensions Not Matching Template](/blog/kdp-cover-dimensions-not-matching-template), [KDP Spine Width Wrong](/blog/kdp-spine-width-wrong), and [How to Fix Barcode Area Contains Text on KDP](/blog/fix-barcode-area-contains-text-kdp).
## Trim Size Requirements
Trim size is the final physical size of the printed book. The PDF must be built around the trim size selected in KDP. Popular sizes include 6 x 9, 8 x 10, 8.5 x 11, 7 x 10, and square formats.
| Trim size | Common use | Main PDF risk |
| 6 x 9 | Novels, nonfiction, memoirs | Margins or gutter too tight after reflow |
| 8 x 10 | Workbooks, activity books, children's books | Artwork near trim or missing bleed |
| 8.5 x 11 | Coloring books, manuals, planners | Large file size and edge-border risk |
| 7 x 10 | Textbooks, guides, premium nonfiction | Cover template mismatch |
| Square formats | Gift books, art books | Cropping and image placement issues |

The mistake is designing in one size and selecting another in KDP. Do not expect KDP to scale the book for you cleanly. Scaling can damage margins, gutters, line thickness, image quality, and safe area.
## Bleed Requirements

Bleed is required when printed artwork needs to reach the physical edge of the page. KDP trims printed pages, and small cutting variation is normal. If a background stops exactly at trim, the finished book can show a white edge. Bleed prevents that by extending artwork past the trim line.

Use bleed for full-page artwork, edge-to-edge photos, black backgrounds, color blocks, children's book spreads, comics, and some coloring pages. Do not use bleed just because it sounds professional. Many novels, journals, workbooks, and puzzle books are better with intentional white margins and no bleed.
Important content should not sit in bleed. Text, page numbers, logos, faces, puzzle clues, and key illustrations should stay inside the safe area. Bleed is for expendable background artwork.

For the full decision framework, read [KDP Bleed vs No Bleed](/blog/kdp-bleed-vs-no-bleed). If you already forgot bleed, see [What Happens If You Forget Bleed on Amazon KDP](/blog/what-happens-if-you-forget-bleed-on-kdp).
## Safe Area Requirements

Safe area is the protected space inside trim where important content belongs. Physical printing and cutting are not pixel-perfect, so KDP expects text and important graphics to stay away from trim and fold edges.

Safe area applies to covers and interiors. On covers, protect titles, subtitles, author names, logos, badges, back-cover blurbs, and spine text. On interiors, protect page numbers, headers, footers, captions, puzzle grids, activity instructions, and borders.

Borders deserve special attention. Thin borders near trim make small cutting variation look obvious. Even if KDP accepts the file, the printed book may look uneven. For border-specific print behavior, see [Why Your KDP Borders Print Unevenly](/blog/kdp-borders-print-unevenly).

For safe-area fundamentals, use [KDP Safe Area Explained](/blog/kdp-safe-area-explained) and [How to Check Safe Area Before Exporting Your KDP Cover](/blog/how-to-check-safe-area-before-exporting-kdp-cover).
## Image Resolution Requirements

KDP print PDFs need images with enough real resolution at final printed size. The common target is about 300 DPI for important raster images. That means a full-page image must have enough pixels for the physical size it occupies.

A 900-pixel image can be fine as a small decoration but poor as a full-page cover. Stretching does not create real detail. AI upscaling can increase pixel count, but it may not fix soft edges, artifacts, or muddy line work.

Vector artwork behaves differently because it can scale cleanly. Rasterized text, screenshots, and flattened low-resolution images do not. If text has been converted into a low-resolution image, it can print blurry even when the PDF itself is large.

To verify resolution, divide image pixels by printed inches. A 6 x 9 full-page image at 300 DPI needs roughly 1800 x 2700 pixels before bleed. An 8.5 x 11 full-page image needs roughly 2550 x 3300 pixels before bleed. For deeper troubleshooting, see [How to Fix Low Resolution Images Errors on Amazon KDP](/blog/fix-low-resolution-images-kdp).
## Font Requirements

Fonts should be embedded in the PDF. Embedding means the PDF carries the font data needed to render text correctly on KDP's systems. If fonts are not embedded, KDP may substitute fonts, shift text, break layout, or reject the file.

In Adobe Acrobat, open File Properties and check the Fonts tab. You want to see embedded or embedded subset. If a font is missing, return to the source file and export again with font embedding enabled.

Some fonts have licensing restrictions that prevent embedding. In that case, use a different licensed font or outline display text carefully. Avoid outlining long body text unless you understand the tradeoffs, because it can increase file size and reduce text editability.
## Color and Print Requirements

Color in print is not identical to color on screen. Screens emit light; printed books reflect light. RGB colors can look brighter on a monitor than on paper. Dark covers and black-background coloring books can print softer, duller, or less saturated than expected.

KDP workflows can accept many files exported from RGB design tools, but creators should still check print contrast. Neon colors, heavy saturation, low-contrast text, black backgrounds, and grayscale interiors need careful review. Matte finishes can soften color further.

For color-shift issues, see [Why Your KDP Cover Colors Look Different After Printing](/blog/kdp-cover-colors-look-different-after-printing). For dark coloring interiors, see [Why Your KDP Coloring Book Prints Too Dark](/blog/kdp-coloring-book-prints-too-dark).
## File Size Requirements
File size is not only about upload speed. A huge PDF can slow KDP processing, freeze Previewer, or fail during upload. But compressing too aggressively can damage print quality.

The best optimization happens before export. Resize images to the actual print size needed. Flatten finished effects when appropriate. Avoid full-page transparent PNGs if a simple flattened page would work. Export once from the source file instead of running the PDF through multiple converters.
If KDP upload fails, read [KDP File Upload Failed](/blog/kdp-file-upload-failed). If upload works but Previewer stalls, read [KDP Previewer Not Loading](/blog/kdp-previewer-not-loading).
## Most Common PDF Mistakes
Here are the top mistakes that cause KDP PDF problems:
1. Designing at the wrong trim size.
2. Selecting the wrong trim size in KDP.
3. Exporting a trim-size PDF when bleed is required.
4. Enabling bleed in KDP without providing a bleed-sized PDF.
5. Putting text or page numbers too close to trim.
6. Using the same gutter for thin and thick books.
7. Designing a cover before final page count is known.
8. Using an old cover template after page count changes.
9. Leaving barcode-area content on the back cover.
10. Stretching low-resolution images.
11. Using screenshots as print artwork.
12. Exporting fonts without embedding.
13. Leaving hidden template marks or layers visible.
14. Uploading a huge, unoptimized Canva PDF.
15. Checking only the design file instead of the exported PDF.
Most of these mistakes are preventable with one habit: verify the final PDF, not only the source layout.
## Coloring Book PDF Requirements

Coloring books have their own PDF risks. Many are single-sided, image-heavy, border-heavy, and built from repeated artwork pages. That makes trim, bleed, safe area, line thickness, and file size especially important.

If illustrations or black backgrounds reach the edge, use bleed correctly. If drawings sit inside white margins, no bleed may be safer. Keep borders well inside trim. Avoid hairline artwork that may print too faintly. Keep color-by-number labels readable and away from edges. Make sure repeated pages do not multiply unnecessary file weight.

Single-sided coloring pages often include blank backs. Check pagination carefully so artwork lands on the intended side. If your coloring book has dark pages, order a proof copy before launch because screen previews do not reveal ink absorption and paper behavior well.
For coloring-book bleed decisions, see [KDP Bleed vs No Bleed for Coloring Books](/blog/kdp-bleed-vs-no-bleed-coloring-books).
## How to Verify a PDF Before Uploading
Use this manual workflow after export:
1. Open the final PDF, not the source file.
2. Check PDF page dimensions in document properties.
3. Compare dimensions against trim size and bleed setting.
4. For covers, compare full wrap size against KDP's cover calculator.
5. Inspect safe area for text, page numbers, borders, and logos.
6. Check gutter on odd and even pages.
7. Confirm fonts are embedded.
8. Check image resolution at final printed size.
9. Remove visible template marks, crop marks, or guide layers.
10. Check barcode area on the back cover.
11. Confirm file size is reasonable for the book type.
12. Upload only the verified export.
This workflow catches far more problems than opening the PDF and glancing at the first page.
## How KDPPreflight Helps
KDPPreflight helps by analyzing the final PDF before upload. It can check trim size, bleed setup, safe-area risks, spine width, cover dimensions, resolution signals, and general PDF readiness.

It does not guarantee approval. Amazon KDP is the final validator, and official requirements can change. But a preflight pass helps you catch common file problems before you spend another upload cycle waiting for KDP Previewer or review.
Use KDPPreflight at the end of the export process. The final PDF is what matters.
## Ultimate Pre-Upload PDF Checklist
Print or save this checklist before every upload:
- Manuscript trim size matches KDP.
- Cover template matches trim, page count, paper type, and binding.
- Interior PDF dimensions match bleed/no-bleed setup.
- Cover PDF is a full wrap, not a front-only image.
- Bleed artwork extends past trim where needed.
- Text and page numbers stay inside safe areas.
- Gutter is wide enough for the page count.
- Borders are not placed near trim.
- Images are high resolution at final print size.
- Fonts are embedded.
- Barcode zone is clear.
- Spine text fits inside the spine safe area.
- Hidden layers and template marks are removed.
- PDF file size is optimized but not over-compressed.
- Final exported PDF has been preflighted.
## Conclusion

KDP PDF requirements are not mysterious once you separate them into production categories: dimensions, bleed, safe area, margins, gutter, images, fonts, color, cover wrap, spine, barcode, file size, and export quality.

The biggest mistake is assuming that a PDF is ready because it opens. KDP needs more than a viewable file. It needs a print-ready file that can survive upload, validation, Previewer rendering, trimming, binding, and review.
Build from the correct trim size, export cleanly, check the final PDF, and validate before upload. That workflow prevents most KDP file problems before Amazon has to catch them.
